abstract: The evolution of behavior is typically attributed to changes in innate circuitry, but learning can also drive behavioral evolution. Mus musculus evolved to produce trimethylamine (TMA) and behaviorally approach it, unlike the ancestral response retained by other mammals including Mus caroli. Here we demonstrate that this attraction is not innate but learned, depending on developmental TMA exposure. Whole brain immediate-early gene mapping reveals experience-dependent patterns of activation in response to TMA olfaction. Using activity-dependent TRAP2 labelling, we find that TMA-responsive neurons in the anterior olfactory nucleus are necessary and sufficient for attraction, consistent with a memory engram. Meanwhile, Mus caroli innate aversion is dependent on excitatory neurons in the posterior cortical amygdala. These results demonstrate how innate and learned circuitry both contribute to behavioral evolution in mammals.
